title: Multi-target regulation of cellular senescence by traditional Chinese medicine: a novel strategy to preventing diabetic kidney disease

sections.abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a common chronic microvascular complication of diabetes and the leading cause of end-stage renal disease. Its pathogenesis is closely linked to cellular senescence. Studies have shown that cellular senescence drives DKD progression via multiple mechanisms, including tubulointerstitial fibrosis, glomerulosclerosis, oxidative stress, and aberrant AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling. However, there remains a lack of specific therapeutic targets or effective drugs for DKD treatment. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), characterized by its multidimensional, multi-target, significant efficacy, and fewer adverse effects, has shown unique advantages in DKD prevention and treatment. This article systematically examines the role of cellular senescence in DKD pathogenesis and, guided by TCM theory, explores how TCM may regulate cellular senescence to mitigate DKD, offering novel perspectives for enhancing clinical management of this condition.
sections.introduction:
Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a common chronic microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus (DM), is characterized by elevated blood glucose levels combined with an abnormal urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio and/or estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). In the United States, >40% of adults with DM develop DKD. In China, the prevalence of DM aged ≥18 years is 11.2%, and the proportion of patients with Type 2 diabetes (T 2 DM) and concomitant DKD is 21.8% [ 1 ]. Existing studies in pathogenesis of DKD have emphasized renal hemodynamic changes, oxidative stress (OS), inflammation, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system overactivity, and cellular senescence [ 2 ]. Consequently, no effective treatments exist and the clinical approach is primarily founded on controlling blood glucose, blood pressure, and blood lipids. Therefore, early screening is crucial for patients at a high risk of DKD, and early detection and timely initiation of renoprotective therapy can reduce morbidity and mortality risk.

Cellular senescence is the basis of organismal aging, a process of gradual decline in cell proliferation, differentiation capacity, and physiological functions [ 3 ]. It is characterized by permanent and irreversible stagnation of the cell cycle, induces inflammation and fibrosis, and is the primary pathogenic mechanism of various chronic diseases. The mechanism underlying renal aging remains unclear, and most existing studies emphasize OS, telomere damage, and aging-related gene expression [ 4 ]. Extensive cellular senescence has been observed in the DKD patients’ renal tissues [ 5 ], and senescence phenotypes such as renal atrophy, tubular fibrosis, and glomerular mesangial hyperplasia have been observed in DKD mice [ 6 ].

Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) attributes DKD to the categories of ‘Thirsty Kidney Disease’ ‘Deficiency’ and ‘Edema’. DKD is mostly triggered by factors such insufficient innate endowment, improper diet, emotional disorder, and overwork, among others. The pathogenesis of DKD in the view point of traditional Chinese medicine is based on deficiency of ‘kidney qi’, and the treatment should focus on ‘tonifying primordial qi’. Some TCM demonstrates significant efficacy in managing chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly against renal fibrosis and DKD. Pharmacological studies have identified multi-targeted mechanisms of herbal bioactive components: Cornus officinalis extract modulates glucose and lipid metabolism, oxidative stress responses, and autophagy [ 7 ]; Poria triterpenoids inhibit TGF-β1/Smad and Wnt/β-catenin profibrotic signaling [ 8 ]; Urushetin attenuates tubular inflammation while enhancing cellular viability [ 9 ]; and bergamot lactone suppresses fibroblast activation through TGF-β1 regulation [ 10 ]. TCM formulations also exhibit synergistic therapeutic effects, such as Taohe Chengqi Decoction’s modulation of proline hydroxylase 2 (PHD2)/UCP1 and receptor-interacting protein kinase-3 (RIPK3)/AKT pathways in fibrosis amelioration [ 11 ], and Shenqi Dihuang Decoction’s preservation of early DKD renal function via anti-inflammatory mechanisms [ 12 ]. It can be seen that as a traditional treasure of Chinese culture, TCM has a potential role in the treatment of DKD, such as favorable curative effects and fewer adverse reactions, based on the holistic concept and criteria of syndrome differentiation and treatment. This article reviews the relationship between cellular senescence and DKD, explores the therapeutic mechanism of TCM in DKD through the regulation of cellular senescence, and provides a reference for researchers and clinicians, less familiar with TCMs.
sections.conclusion:
Cellular senescence is a primary pathogenic mechanism of DKD. With the advancement of clinical research, an increasing amount of objective evidence indicates that TCM can regulates cell senescence to treat DKD. This paper systematically explains TCM’s multi-target mechanisms against cellular senescence in DKD, mainly involving telomere repair, autophagy activation, senescence-related genes activation, and oxidative stress mitigation. There are complex interactions between the mechanisms. Specifically, oxidative stress, as a core driver, can accelerate telomere shortening though DNA oxidative damage, and inhibit autophagy leading to the accumulation of damaged mitochondria, exacerbating ROS accumulation and thus inducing cellular senescence. In addition, the antioxidant system maintains autophagy function by protecting autophagy-related proteins, while autophagy inhibition can weaken the cell’s ability to remove oxidative damage products. TCM can reduce the attack of ROS on telomeres and mitochondria through its antioxidant components (e.g. activation of Nrf2 pathway), activate AMPK/mTOR-dependent autophagic flow to remove the damaged substances, regulate telomerase activity to delay telomere depletion, and synergistically inhibit the expression of senescence-related genes, such as p53 and p16. TCM’s multi-pathway strategy effectively restores cellular homeostasis and decelerates senescence progression, offering novel therapeutic perspectives for DKD management.

Current research on TCM in the field of cellular senescence in DKD still has significant limitations. First, the available evidence mainly comes from animal and cellular experiments, and clinical studies are mostly limited to small-sample observational trials, lacking multicenter RCTs and long-term follow-up data, as well as insufficient evidence-based medical evidence, which can not provide empirical and theoretical support for the clinical treatment of human beings. Second, the assessment of efficacy still relies on traditional renal function indicators (e.g. eGFR, urinary protein), and fail to integrate specific markers of cellular senescence such as plasma SASP factor and the proportion of p16 INK4a -positive cells, which makes it difficult to accurately assess the anti-aging effects of TCM. Third, the heterogeneity of the studies was prominent, and the lack of uniformity in the aging models used in different experiments led to insufficient comparability of conclusions.

In the future, prospective cohort studies or multi-center double-blind RCTs with larger sample sizes are needed to dynamically monitor changes in serum SASP factor levels, elucidating the quantitative and efficacy relationships between TCM interventions and aging markers. We can also utilize single-cell sequencing, metabolomics of intestinal flora and machine modeling algorithms to reveal the multi-target regulatory mechanisms of TCM and construct efficacy prediction models. In addition, it is also necessary to establish disease-specific standardized aging models and develop unified aging assessment standards. Notably, there is still a gap in the field of regulating DKD cellular senescence by external TCM therapies such as acupuncture and tuina, and it is recommended that relevant basic and clinical studies be conducted in the future to enrich the therapeutic connotation of TCM.
